title: Car Charging Stations
desc: Plan, site and run a small public or shared EV charging point: demand, power, safety, pricing, uptime and users.
outcomes: Explain charger types, connectors and grid limits.
Choose a site and size the supply.
Judge safety, cost, uptime and fairness.
Write a site plan and operations sheet.
task: Plan one charging point or small hub with site survey, power sizing, safety plan, tariff, maintenance plan and 12-month cash view.
condition: A computer, a map, a spreadsheet, two peers and a licensed electrician mentor. No live installation work is done by learners.
standard: Power and demand maths is correct; protective devices and earthing are listed and approved by a licensed person; accessibility is planned; uptime target and tariff shown; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Site hosts, shop and hotel owners, utilities assistants, installers.
evidence: site survey, sizing sheet, safety plan, tariff, maintenance plan, cash view
modules: Charger types and connectors
Understand
Chargers differ in power, speed and cost. Choose by how long drivers will stay.
AC points (3 to 22 kW) suit long stays such as homes, workplaces and hotels; the car converts AC to DC.
DC fast chargers (50 kW and above) suit quick stops on routes.
Connector types and standards depend on region; check which cars you must support.
Smart chargers can share power and report faults.
A shopping mall installs 7 kW points because shoppers stay about two hours and add 14 kWh each. A highway site installs 60 kW units because drivers want 30 kWh in 30 minutes.
Compare three charger types in a table with power, time to add 30 kWh, cost range and best site.
Table values are correct and sourced.
Choosing a site
Apply
The right place and the right grid connection decide success.
Visible, safe, well lit, accessible, near amenities such as food and toilets.
Distance to the electricity supply and spare transformer capacity.
Permission from the land owner, the utility and the local authority.
Space for growth and for queuing.
A site 20 m from the main panel saves cable cost; another 300 m away needs trenching and a new transformer, doubling cost.
Do a mock site survey for two sites and score five criteria.
Scores justified in writing.
Power sizing and load management
Apply
Do not overload the supply.
Total kW = number of chargers x kW x diversity factor.
Compare with supply capacity; use load management when limited.
Plan growth with spare conduit.
Include power for lights and equipment.
Four 7 kW points on a 20 kW supply use load sharing so that total draw never exceeds 20 kW; with all four in use each car gets about 5 kW.
Size a site and show the calculation.
Maths correct; supply limit respected.
Demand and revenue
Analyse
Estimate real use before you invest.
Count nearby EVs and traffic; talk to likely users.
Utilisation = hours in use / hours open.
Revenue = kWh sold x price minus electricity cost and fees.
Test low, medium and high demand cases.
At 15 per cent utilisation a 7 kW point sells about 25 kWh a day; at 5 per cent it sells about 8 kWh a day and may not break even.
Build a 12-month model with three demand cases.
Currency shown and assumptions listed.
Safety and standards
Evaluate
Protect users and property.
Residual current protection, earthing, surge protection, emergency stop and fire plan.
Weather protection, cable management and trip-free layout.
Regular inspection and testing by qualified staff.
Clear signs and instructions.
A charger fails an earth test and is locked out until a licensed electrician repairs it; the fault is logged.
List the safety measures for your site.
A licensed person approves the list.
Pricing and payment
Evaluate
Make prices clear and fair.
Per kWh, per minute, session fee and idle fee.
Display price before charging begins.
Use payment methods approved in your place.
Offer a way for users without a smartphone.
An idle fee after 30 minutes frees the bay for other drivers, and users are told by a sign and a message.
Design a tariff and test it with three examples.
Examples worked correctly.
Operations and uptime
Apply
Chargers must work when drivers arrive.
Remote monitoring and a fault response target.
Maintenance schedule and spare parts.
A helpline number printed on the unit.
Record faults and fixes.
A target to fix faults within 24 hours is met 95 per cent of the time by keeping spare connectors on site.
Write an operations sheet with targets.
Targets are measurable.
Inclusion and the site plan
Create
Everyone should be able to charge.
Step-free access, bay width, lighting and a call button.
Multi-language instructions and simple screens.
Share the plan with the community.
Review after six months.
Wider bays and a call button let wheelchair users charge independently.
Finish the plan.
Peers can follow the plan and see accessibility steps.
quiz: What is load sharing?
Dividing supply among chargers. (Covered in module 1: Charger types. To pass that module: Table includes time to add 30 kWh.)
Which suits long stays?
AC chargers. (Covered in module 2: Site choice. To pass that module: Scores for 5 criteria.)
Utilisation formula?
Hours in use / hours open. (Covered in module 3: Power sizing. To pass that module: Maths correct.)
Name a safety measure.
RCD, earthing or emergency stop. (Covered in module 4: Demand and revenue. To pass that module: Currency shown.)
Why display price?
Fairness and trust. (Covered in module 5: Safety and standards. To pass that module: Approved by licensed person.)
What is idle fee?
Charge for occupying a bay after charging. (Covered in module 6: Pricing and payment. To pass that module: Examples worked.)
Who approves electrics?
Licensed electrician. (Covered in module 7: Operations and uptime. To pass that module: Targets measurable.)
Why monitor remotely?
Quick faults response. (Covered in module 8: Inclusion and plan. To pass that module: Peers can follow it.)
Name an access feature.
Step-free route or wide bays. (Covered in module 8: Inclusion and plan. To pass that module: Peers can follow it.)
Revenue formula?
kWh x price minus cost. (Covered in module 8: Inclusion and plan. To pass that module: Peers can follow it.)

ladder: Charger types

L1: learner can name charger types. Focus module: Charger types (Understand, 3 h). Slow, fast and ultra-fast. Key points: AC points (3 to 22 kW) suit long stays; DC fast chargers suit quick stops. Connectors and standards depend on region. Smart chargers share load.

Teach: open with the worked example. A mall installs 7 kW points because shoppers stay two hours. Then set the activity: Compare 3 charger types. Mark against the standard: Table includes time to add 30 kWh. Check at this level: What is load sharing? Model answer: Dividing supply among chargers. Table.
Site choice

L2: learner knows safety basics. Focus module: Site choice (Apply, 4 h). Right place, right grid. Key points: Visible, safe, lit, accessible, near amenities. Distance to the electricity supply; transformer capacity. Permissions from the owner and the utility.

Teach: open with the worked example. A site 20 m from the panel cuts cable cost. Then set the activity: Do a mock site survey. Mark against the standard: Scores for 5 criteria. Check at this level: Which suits long stays? Model answer: AC chargers. Safety.
Power sizing

L3: learner can survey a site. Focus module: Power sizing (Apply, 5 h). Do not overload the supply. Key points: Total kW = chargers x kW x diversity factor. Check supply capacity; add load management if limited. Plan growth.

Teach: open with the worked example. Four 7 kW points on a 20 kW supply use load sharing. Then set the activity: Size your site. Mark against the standard: Maths correct. Check at this level: Utilisation formula? Model answer: Hours in use / hours open. Survey.
Demand and revenue

L4: learner can run a site. Focus module: Demand and revenue (Analyse, 5 h). Estimate real use. Key points: Count nearby EVs and traffic. Utilisation = hours in use / hours open. Revenue = kWh sold x price minus electricity cost.

Teach: open with the worked example. At 15% utilisation a 7 kW point sells about 9 kWh a day. Then set the activity: Build a 12-month model. Mark against the standard: Currency shown. Check at this level: Name a safety measure. Model answer: RCD, earthing or emergency stop. Ops.
Safety and standards

L5: learner can model demand. Focus module: Safety and standards (Evaluate, 5 h). Protect users. Key points: RCD protection, earthing, surge, emergency stop, fire plan. Weather protection and cable management. Regular inspection.

Teach: open with the worked example. A charger fails a test and is locked out until fixed. Then set the activity: List safety measures. Mark against the standard: Approved by licensed person. Check at this level: Why display price? Model answer: Fairness and trust. Model.
Operations and uptime

L6: learner can lead a small team. Focus module: Operations and uptime (Apply, 4 h). Chargers must work. Key points: Remote monitoring; a fault response time. Maintenance schedule; spares. Helpline number on the unit.

Teach: open with the worked example. A 24-hour fix target is met 95% of the time. Then set the activity: Write an operations sheet. Mark against the standard: Targets measurable. Check at this level: What is idle fee? Model answer: Charge for occupying a bay after charging. Team.
Inclusion and plan

L7: learner can audit a site plan. Focus module: Inclusion and plan (Create, 4 h). Everyone should be able to charge. Key points: Step-free access, bay width, lighting. Multi-language instructions. Share the plan with the community.

Teach: open with the worked example. Wider bays and a call button suit wheelchair users. Then set the activity: Finish the plan. Mark against the standard: Peers can follow it. Check at this level: Who approves electrics? Model answer: Licensed electrician. Peer audit.
